subtype: Parents × Divorce or conflict at home [Receiver]
passage:
A kettle screaming at midnight while Ammi and Abbu shouted in the next room: that's the sound I still hear. I'm Nazia, and I'm telling you this, Bidisha, because you asked why I go quiet when couples argue in the canteen.

They separated last year. At first I tried to fix it. I carried messages. Abbu said, "Tell your mother," and Ammi said, "Tell your father," and I felt like a bridge with both ends on fire. I even wrote each of them a long letter about being kinder.

Then my aunt said, "You're their daughter, not their referee." It was the first time I could breathe.

I stopped carrying messages. I call both of them every Sunday and tell each I love them and won't discuss the other. It still hurts. But I sleep now.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel while carrying messages between her parents?
qa.a: Like a bridge with both ends on fire, pulled and burned from both sides.

qa.q: What boundary did Nazia set with her parents?
qa.a: She stopped carrying messages, kept calling both every Sunday, and told each of them she loves them but will not discuss the other.

qa.q: What did Nazia's aunt see that Nazia hadn't?
qa.a: That Nazia was taking on a job that belonged to the parents, being their referee instead of their daughter.

grounding: Nazia's parents' fights and separation land on her; she stops trying to fix them and loves both while keeping healthy distance.

subtype: Parents × Divorce or conflict at home [Receiver]
passage:
Sunday night, hostel
Went home for the weekend. Mistake. Papa and Mummy didn't speak at lunch, then shouted about money at dinner. Manoj, fifteen, put his earphones in and stared at his plate.
Afterwards Mummy came to my room and cried about Papa for an hour. Then Papa caught me on the stairs: "You're old enough now. Tell her she's being unreasonable." I nearly did. For a second I wanted to pick a side just to make the noise stop.
I didn't. I said, "Papa, I love you both. I'm not going to carry messages. Please talk to someone, a counsellor, anyone." He looked hurt. So did I, probably.
I took Manoj for a walk to the chai stall and told him none of this is our fault, and that he can call me any night. On the bus back I felt guilty for leaving, and relieved too. Both.
— Hemant

qa.q: What did Papa ask Hemant to tell Mummy?
What did Hemant feel on the bus back to the hostel?
qa.a: Guilty for leaving and relieved at the same time.

qa.q: How did Hemant avoid taking a side?
qa.a: By refusing to carry messages, telling Papa that Hemant loves them both, suggesting a counsellor, and reassuring Manoj that it isn't their fault.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj at home?
qa.a: Tense and lonely; he shuts out the fights with earphones and needs to hear that none of it is his fault.

grounding: Shows parents' fights landing on a young adult, who refuses to take a side, loves both and keeps a healthy distance while supporting a younger sibling.

Parul: did you see what papa posted on the family group
Vaibhav: yeah. i left the group for a bit
Parul: mummy's been crying all day. you should call papa and tell him off
Vaibhav: i'm not doing that
Parul: so you're on his side??
Vaibhav: no. i'm not on any side. they're separating. it's their decision, not ours to fix
Parul: easy for you to say from hostel
Vaibhav: fair. it's not easy. i called mummy this morning and papa last night. i love them both
Vaibhav: i just won't be the messenger
Parul: i feel like i have to hold everything together here
Vaibhav: you don't. that's not your job either
Vaibhav: want me to come home this weekend? movie, just us
Parul: ...yes please 🥺
Vaibhav: booking the bus now

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do after seeing Papa's post?
qa.a: Left the family group for a bit.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav feel about being pulled into the conflict?
qa.a: Torn and sad ("it's not easy"), loving both parents yet determined not to become the messenger.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav keep a healthy distance without abandoning Parul?
qa.a: Vaibhav refused to take sides or carry messages, called both parents, told Parul it isn't Parul's job either, and offered to come home for a movie.

qa.q: How might Parul see Vaibhav's refusal at first?
qa.a: As siding with Papa, and easy to do from the hostel; later Parul is relieved that Vaibhav is coming home.

grounding: Illustrates parents' separation pulling siblings into the conflict, and choosing to love both parents without taking a side or fixing it.
